newsitem.title: USA: IBM sees strong 1997 business PC market.
newsitem.headline: IBM sees strong 1997 business PC market.

text.p: LAS VEGAS, Nov 19 - The general manager of International Business Machines Corp's personal computer business said he expected the business computer market to remain strong next year, helped by upgrades of Microsoft's Windows NT.
"The corporate (market) could continue to be strong," Samuel Palmisano of the IBM Personal Computer Co, said in a presentation at the Comdex trade show in Las Vegas.
Palmisano said the market may not grow in 1997 at the recent 17 to 18 percent unit rate, but 14 to 15 percent growth next year would represent a strong number off a larger base.
He said the corporate market has been growing by an estimated 16-19 percent. "We've been cliping along at a better pace than that," he said of IBM's business.

There had been concern when after seasonal slowness in Europe in July and August, the corporate market did not bounce back in September, but Palmisano said, "We've had a very strong performance in October and November" in Europe.
"The U.S. continues to be strong all year. Asia is booming," he said, including growth rates in Japan's corporate sector that exceeded 70 percent in the third quarter.
But he said the outlook was still uncertain for the PC industry's U.S. retail sales in the critical pre-holiday selling period, although IBM's consumer business remained strong.
"Our Aptiva consumer business is growing at an incredible rate of growth," he said. But, he noted, there is a lot of caution now on the U.S. retail side."

Palmisano cited recent price cuts by rival Compaq Computer Corp just ahead of the pre-Christmas selling period as an unfavorable sign, although he said the move may also indicate that Compaq built "too much relative to what's been flying off the shelves."
Palmisano said he took a conservative approach to future trends in IBM sales.
"Second (quarter) was great. Third was brilliant. These strengths continue through the year," he said. "However I have to warn you we are in a weekly business."
